title: Mobile connectivity is widening financial access while digital safety, gender, income, and resilience gaps remain
source_unit: World Bank, Global Findex Database 2025: Connectivity and Financial Inclusion in the Digital Economy
geography: 141 economies, based on nationally representative surveys conducted in 2024

denominator.unit: economies covered by nationally representative Global Findex surveys

global_account_ownership.unit: percent of adults globally with a financial account in 2024

global_account_ownership_2021.unit: percent of adults globally with a financial account in 2021

global_mobile_phone_ownership.unit: percent of adults globally owning a mobile phone

observations.method: World Bank Global Findex nationally representative demand-side surveys measuring account ownership and mobile-phone access.
observations.uncertainty: Country coverage, survey timing, definitions, and population weights affect comparability; account ownership and phone ownership do not establish effective use, affordability, or welfare gains.
observations.subgroup: Adults across low-, middle-, and high-income economies, including women, poorer adults, and people with limited digital access.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rising account ownership can reflect payment digitization or policy enrollment without increasing savings, control, privacy, or financial security; mobile access can also introduce new fraud and dependency risks.

denominator.unit: economies covered by the Global Findex 2025 survey frame

digital_merchant_payments.unit: percent of adults making digital merchant payments in 2024

lmics_mobile_money_saving.unit: percent of adults in developing economies using a mobile-money account to save in 2024

lmics_mobile_money_saving_2021.unit: percentage-point increase in the share using mobile-money accounts to save since 2021

observations.method: World Bank comparison of digital merchant payments and mobile-money saving across survey rounds and economy groups.
observations.uncertainty: Payment and saving measures capture reported behavior, not balances, returns, quality, or whether digital use displaced safer or more affordable alternatives.
observations.subgroup: Adults in developing economies, mobile-money users, merchants, account holders, and people using digital payments or savings tools.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital payments may increase convenience and formal access while shifting costs, fraud exposure, data extraction, or pressure to transact onto consumers.

denominator.unit: global and low- and middle-income adult population comparisons in Global Findex 2025

lmics_women_account_ownership.unit: percent of women in low- and middle-income economies with a financial account in 2024

lmics_women_formal_saving.unit: percent of women in low- and middle-income economies using formal saving in 2024

lmics_women_digital_payments.unit: percent of women in low- and middle-income economies making or receiving digital payments in 2024

unaccounted_women.unit: millions of women worldwide without a financial account

observations.method: World Bank gender- and income-disaggregated analysis of account ownership, formal saving, digital payments, and access gaps.
observations.uncertainty: Group averages conceal country, household, age, disability, rurality, documentation, and intra-household-control differences; access does not equal independent control or benefit.
observations.subgroup: Women, men, poorer adults, low- and middle-income economies, account holders, and financially excluded adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: Gender gaps may narrow through mobile money and payment systems while persisting in phone ownership, identification, privacy, bargaining power, literacy, safety, and product quality.

denominator.unit: economies covered by the Global Findex 2025 digital-connectivity and financial-health measures

unbanked_without_phone.unit: percent of adults without financial accounts in low- and middle-income economies who also do not own a mobile phone

south_asia_subsaharan_unbanked_without_p.unit: approximately share of unaccounted adults in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa who also lack a mobile phone

financial_resilience.value: the share of financially resilient adults in low- and middle-income economies held broadly steady since 2021

digital_safety.value: the database adds globally comparable indicators on phone security, internet use, and digital safety

observations.method: World Bank Digital Connectivity Tracker and financial-health indicators combined with account, payment, saving, and borrowing measures.
observations.uncertainty: Digital-safety indicators are early cross-country measures and do not capture all harms, institutional remedies, or long-run resilience; financial resilience is a broad capacity measure rather than observed shock recovery.
observations.subgroup: Unbanked adults, people without phones, women and poorer adults, rural and low-connectivity populations, and adults managing major expenses or income loss.
observations.counterinterpretation: A phone or account can be an enabler without being sufficient for resilience; social networks, public transfers, employment, health, and consumer protection remain part of the buffer.

related_sources.claim: The Global Findex financial-health chapter provides complementary resilience and risk-management measures.
The Global Findex 2025 report provides the primary survey frame and chapter structure.

boundary: This record adds a global connectivity-to-financial-inclusion route linking mobile access, accounts, payments, saving, gender and income gaps, digital safety, and financial resilience. It uses aggregate publication findings from nationally representative surveys, not respondent-level analysis, personal transaction records, causal welfare estimates, or claims that digital finance automatically improves household security.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank Global Findex 2025 report, database page, financial-inclusion chapters, and data-download materials were checked for the survey frame, connectivity, payment, saving, gender, exclusion, digital-safety, and resilience claims.
